extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, dramatists, and students of poetry/drama
extracted.subtask_description: Classical guidance for composing and evaluating tragedy: plot construction (recognition, reversal, complication/unravelling), characterization, diction, and staging. Focused on creating convincing dramatic effect and preserving artistic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the type and ennoble it
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet, in representing men who are irascible or indolent, or have other defects of character, should preserve the type and yet ennoble it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the essential character-type intact while elevating it artistically (e.g., the portrayals of Achilles by Agathon and Homer). Avoid caricature that loses the dignity or poetic worth of the type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals to the senses as concomitants of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses are not among the essentials but are concomitants of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sensory appeals matter and leave room for error; employ them carefully as supplements to the essential elements of poetry (see more in treatises on sensory representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by signs/tokens (least artistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by signs: congenital signs (e.g., a spear borne by a race) or acquired bodily marks or external tokens (scars, necklaces, little ark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the least artistic mode of recognition—formal proof or tokens used expressly for discovery are less subtle. Examples: Odysseus’ scar (nurse vs. swineherds' different modes of discovery). Use of tokens for mere proof is a lower form of artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by a turn of incident (superior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition which comes about by a turn of incident (e.g., the Bath Scene in the Odyssey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered a better and more artistic kind of recognition because it arises naturally from events rather than contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition invented by the poet (artificial, deficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions invented at will by the poet and therefore wanting in art (e.g., Orestes in Iphigenia realizing he is Orestes by speaking himself rather than plot necessity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making characters announce knowledge the plot doesn't require; such devices feel like authorial fiat rather than organic discovery and are akin to the earlier fault of contrived tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by memory (evoked by sight or sound)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that depends on memory—sight or hearing recalls the past and produces recognition (e.g., hero breaks into tears on seeing a picture, or hears a minstrel and weeps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory-evoked recollection to produce plausible, emotionally grounded discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by process of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by a character’s reasoning: making natural inferences (e.g., 'Some one resembling me has come; no one resembles me but Orestes; therefore Orestes has come').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This kind is based on plausible inference from available evidence; when natural, it is an effective and artistic device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite recognition involving false inference
rubrics_metrics.description: A composite kind where a character makes a false inference expecting another to react (e.g., disguised Odysseus imagines A will recognise the bow though A never saw it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relies on expectation and can produce recognition by deception but is a problematic form—recognition achieved through false inference is less sound artistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best recognition: arises from incidents themselves (natural means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all recognitions, the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves, where the startling discovery is made by natural means (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigenia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for recognitions that are intrinsic to the action and thus believable without tokens or artificial contrivances; these dispense with external aids and feel inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize the scene (place the scene before your eyes)
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the plot and working it out with the proper diction, the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing everything vividly like a spectator helps pick consistent actions and avoid oversights (example: Carcinus’ failure when a stage situation was mis-seen). This reduces inconsistencies and stage implausibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work out appropriate gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should work out his play, to the best of his power, with appropriate gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gestures must suit the characters and situations; planning physical expression enhances believability and the connection between inner emotion and outward action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors must feel and show genuine emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who feel emotion are most convincing through natural sympathy with the characters they represent; one who is agitated storms, one who is angry rages, with most life-like reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conviction requires either a natural gift (ability to take the mould of character) or an intense strain resembling madness; natural sympathy produces the most convincing performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch general outline first, then fill episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poet takes the story ready-made or constructs it, he should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the overall shape (illustrated by Iphigenia) so that incidents later added fit the plan; avoid letting extraneous motives or outside events undermine the central action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be relevant to the action
rubrics_metrics.description: After the general plan, fill in episodes—these must be relevant to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drama episodes are short but should contribute to the action (example: Orestes’ madness and purificatory rite are relevant episodes). Irrelevant episode-extensions belong to epic expansion, not tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy structure: Complication and Unravelling (Dénouement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts—Complication and Unravelling (Dénouement). Incidents extraneous to the action are frequently combined with a portion of the action proper to form the Complication; the rest is the Unravelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and design where the turning-point occurs (end of Complication) and where the change begins (start of Unravelling). Maintain unity so these parts work together toward the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Complication
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Complication I mean all that extends from the beginning of the action to the part which marks the turning-point to good or bad fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose the Complication to set up the reversal/turning-point clearly and causally; it should prepare the inevitable change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Unravelling (Denouement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unravelling is that which extends from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Unravelling should follow naturally from the turning-point and carry through to a coherent conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Tragedy: Complex, Pathetic, Ethical, Simple
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of Tragedy: the Complex (depending on Reversal and Recognition), the Pathetic (motive is passion), the Ethical (motives are ethical), and the Simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the dominant organizing principle of your tragedy and select devices appropriate to that kind. The poet should, if possible, combine elements; avoid reducing play to spectacle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex tragedy relies on Reversal and Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Complex depends entirely on Reversal of the Situation and Recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reversals and recognitions to be causal and natural, achieving powerful tragic effects when properly combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude purely spectacular elements
rubrics_metrics.description: We exclude the purely spectacular element (exemplified by the Phorcides, Prometheus, scenes in Hades).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle alone does not make a good tragedy; prioritize plot, reversal, and recognition over mere stage effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine the greatest and most important poetic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should endeavour, if possible, to combine all poetic elements; or failing that, the greatest number and those the most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics expect excellence across elements—aim to integrate plot, thought, diction, spectacle, song, and character to the extent possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plot identity test for sameness/difference
rubrics_metrics.description: In speaking of a tragedy as the same or different, the best test is the plot—identity exists where the Complication and Unravelling are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether two tragedies are effectively the same by comparing their core plot-structure (Complication + Unravelling), not superficial elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making an Epic structure into a Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make an Epic structure into a Tragedy—an Epic structure has a multiplicity of plots; drama should select portions rather than dramatise the whole tale (e.g., whole Iliad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy requires unity and appropriate scale—select a part of a larger story to dramatize rather than trying to encompass an epic's full scope; failure often follows from trying to dramatize entire epics or multiple large plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integral actor sharing the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole, and share in the action (in the manner of Sophocles rather than Euripides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choral songs that are mere interludes unrelated to the subject; the Chorus should participate in and advance the dramatic action rather than interrupt it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought: effects produced by speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Thought is included every effect which has to be produced by speech—the subdivisions being argument and refutation; the excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger); and the suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design speeches to produce these effects; apply rhetorical principles (see Rhetoric) to craft arguments, excite emotions, and convey significance in dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic incidents should speak for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic incidents must be treated so that they speak for themselves without verbal exposition; effects aimed at in speech should be produced by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer showing over telling: let actions carry meaning and emotional effect; speeches should enhance and produce thought, not merely narrate what incidents already show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of utterance belong to Delivery (not strictly poet’s art)
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch treats Modes of Utterance (command, prayer, statement, threat, question, answer), but this province belongs to the art of Delivery and masters of that science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the poet should know the kinds of utterance, fine-grained delivery (intonation, rhetorical performance) is a performer's/artisan's domain; avoid blaming poet for performative faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be versed in language parts relevant to diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Language includes Letter, Syllable; Connecting word, Noun, Verb, Inflexion or Case, Sentence or Phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet should understand these elements—letters (vowels, semi-vowels, mutes), syllables, connecting words, nouns, verbs, inflexions, and sentences—because diction and metre depend on them; detailed metrical and phonetic matters belong to specialists on metre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and choose word-types and styles deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word is current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, or altered; words are simple, double/compound, triple, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate in diction choice (current vs. strange, literal vs. metaphorical, newly coined forms). Use compound forms and ornamental language appropriately for effect and unity.
